preamble: Eleven solutions are of a kind, hinted at but not defined.

clue.text: pi ?!

parts.note: surface reading: the Greek letter or the circle constant, followed by a puzzled ?!
setter's reading: the clue is the result of obeying an instruction, and the solver must find the instruction that produces these two letters

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read TURN IP as an instruction and IP turned round becomes PI, the whole clue. The preamble says the vegetable answers are not defined, so nothing else is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: There is no definition by design; the preamble tells solvers that eleven answers belong to one unnamed category, here root crops.

clue.text: Bird in celebrity magazine putting on outer garments

indicators.note: something put on as an outer layer surrounds whatever is beneath it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: wear means clothing, as in menswear or sportswear
Heat is a British celebrity gossip magazine

explanation.surface: A bird photographed for a celebrity magazine has been dressed up in clothes for the shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Heat is a British weekly gossip magazine, and wear is the retail word for clothing, as in menswear. 'Bird in' sounds like the bird is featured, but 'in' only joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The wheatear is a small migratory songbird of open country, related to chats and thrushes.

clue.text: Formation of tornado in southern April storms

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for southern

indicators.note: to storm is to rage and churn about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A weather report on a twister forming during spring storms in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storms' reads as a noun in the weather picture but works as a verb signalling the rearrangement of the month's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado takes the shape of a rotating funnel, so its form is described as a spiral or vortex.

clue.text: Lays blame over …

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to pin the rap on someone is an idiom for blaming them

explanation.surface: Someone accusing another and then trailing off mid-sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: PINS RAP read backwards gives PARSNIP. The rap is slang for blame or a criminal charge; the vegetable itself is left undefined, as the preamble promises.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given by design; the preamble says eleven answers share one unnamed category, and this pale root crop belongs to it.

clue.text: … container container container container of nothing

definitions.note: a noun phrase for an adjective: read as 'holding nothing'

indicators.note: here the word acts as a verb, something that holds the next item inside it

parts.note: a vat is a large tank for liquids
a can is a tin or metal pot

explanation.surface: A stammering continuation of the clue above, repeating one word four times.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word plays three different roles: a tank, a verb meaning 'holding', and a tin, before the last repeat opens the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vacant is empty, holding no contents or occupants at all.

clue.text: Trump started to live, excluded, away from home at first

indicators.note: this phrase puts its piece at the front of the answer

parts.note: someone away from home is out

indicators.note: what is excluded is shut out, so those letters are removed from the word

parts.note: begun is the past participle of begin
to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: A news line about Trump starting to live somewhere, shut out and away from home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' looks like the politician but is the verb meaning beat. 'Excluded' looks like a description but tells you to drop the 'to live' letters from 'started'.
explanation.definitionFit: To trump an opponent is to beat them, and to outgun is to overpower with greater firepower or ability.

clue.text: Apes?!

parts.note: surface reading: monkeys or great apes, with a startled ?!
setter's reading: the clue is the output of a shuffling instruction, and the solver must find the phrase that would produce these letters

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: MUSHY is read as an anagram signal and PEAS as its fodder, and PEAS mashed up gives APES. Mushy peas are mashed marrowfat peas, a British chip-shop side dish.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble names a hidden category of eleven answers, and this mashed pea side dish fits it.

clue.text: Faint with illness after vegetable starter

indicators.note: coming after places this piece behind the other one
a starter comes at the beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word
ague is an old word for a malarial fever with shivering

explanation.surface: Someone feeling faint and ill after eating a vegetable starter at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faint' looks like fainting from illness, but it is the adjective meaning indistinct. 'Vegetable starter' sounds like a first course, yet it supplies just one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint outline or memory is unclear and hazy, which is what vague means.

clue.text: Lunatic unmanned? Not in this puzzle!

definitions.text: Lunatic unmanned? Not in this puzzle!

parts.note: surface reading: something to do with the moon with nobody aboard, like a robotic lunar probe
setter's reading: the grid slot that usually opens a crossword is missing here, as the first across entry in this grid is numbered seven

explanation.walkthrough: This grid has no 1-across: the first across light is 7. So ONE ACROSS is the very thing absent from this puzzle, an unoccupied slot.
explanation.definitionFit: Most crosswords open with a clue numbered one in the across list, but this particular grid starts its across numbering later.

clue.text: Island escape

parts.note: the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea
to get out is to escape

explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is a British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea; MAN plus GET OUT gives MANGETOUT, a flat pea pod eaten whole.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble says eleven answers share a hidden category, and this edible pea pod belongs.

clue.text: Good god!

parts.note: OK means fine, acceptable
Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good god!' reads as an oath, but each word gives letters. Ra is the crossword's favourite god.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble hides the category, and this green seed pod, also called ladies' fingers, fits.

clue.text: Charm unhealthy pal into eating vegetable

indicators.note: to eat something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within the other
something unhealthy is in poor shape, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a pea is a vegetable

explanation.surface: Trying to win over a sickly friend who is into eating vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: PAL is rearranged to APL, which then holds PEA: AP-PEA-L.
explanation.definitionFit: Charm and appeal are both nouns for an attractive quality that draws people in.

clue.text: Support for essentials of writer's home: king's copper penny

parts.note: someone at home is in
K for king, plus the S of the possessive
copper and tan are both reddish-brown colours
d stood for penny in old British money, from the Latin denarius

explanation.surface: A note on a writer's household, mentioning a king and a copper coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'penny' together suggest a coin, but copper is a colour here and penny the old abbreviation d.
explanation.definitionFit: An inkstand is a desk stand holding ink bottles and pens, the basic tools a writer once needed.

clue.text: See 16
Cash in chips at the casino? You might need this

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to cash in one's chips is an idiom for passing away

definitions.text: at the casino? You might need this
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a small numbered cube thrown in gambling games such as craps

explanation.surface: A gambler exchanging chips for money at a casino, with a wink at what they need.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash in chips' looks like a literal casino act, but it is the idiom for death.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to expire, matching the idiom, and the noun is the singular of dice used at gaming tables.

clue.text: Vehicle disintegrates

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
rots means decays, falls apart

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vehicle disintegrates' reads as a rusting car, which is exactly the wordplay; the vegetable itself is never defined.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble groups eleven answers in one hidden category, and these orange roots belong.

clue.text: Metal image of God reputedly placed above a South American city

indicators.note: in a down entry, what is placed above comes first in the reading order

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
Genesis says humans were made in God's image
taken as written

explanation.surface: A metal religious statue mounted over a city in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal image of God' wants to be a statue, but metal and image split: copper's symbol, then humankind.
explanation.definitionFit: Cumaná is a coastal city in eastern Venezuela, among the oldest European-founded settlements on the continent.

clue.text: Tell diner about …

indicators.note: about can mean moved around, so the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Telling a customer in a restaurant about something, trailing off into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it signals the rearrangement of the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble hides the category, and this orange split pulse used in dal belongs to it.

clue.text: See 10
Boatman gets sack in church

indicators.note: being in a place means being enclosed by it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: getting something adds it on, so one piece joins the next

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
a sack is a bag

explanation.surface: The setter, Boatman, is dismissed while in church.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is this puzzle's setter, so the surface is a joke at his own expense; the name just means a sailor, AB. 'Gets sack' looks like being fired, but sack is a bag.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble names a hidden category of eleven, and this leafy head vegetable fits.

clue.text: … startling horse eaten by naughty goblin

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater
a naughty creature misbehaves, so its letters do not stay in line

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse

explanation.surface: A frightening scene of a mischievous goblin devouring a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, a common crossword source for two letters. The ellipsis just carries on the sentence from the clue before.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mind-boggling astonishes and staggers the mind, so it is startling.

clue.text: Fight off engineer over vegetable

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece placed over another reads first

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army corps
a pulse is an edible seed such as a lentil or bean

explanation.surface: An engineer battling over a vegetable, as at an allotment dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers, abbreviated RE, are a stock crossword source for 'engineer'.
explanation.definitionFit: To repulse an attack is to drive it back, the same as fending or beating it off.

clue.text: Bedlam as Spooner ate rodent

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: had means ate, and a mouse is a rodent; swap the first sounds

explanation.surface: Chaos breaks out as Reverend Spooner eats a rat.
explanation.walkthrough: HAD MOUSE with its opening sounds exchanged becomes MAD HOUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedlam, named after a London asylum, means uproar and chaos, as does a madhouse.

clue.text: Too much wave motion beneath one

indicators.note: in a down entry, what lies beneath comes later in the reading order

parts.note: a means one, as in a single thing
a swell is the heaving of the sea in long waves

explanation.surface: A seasick complaint: there is too much rolling of the waves under someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too much' looks like one phrase but splits: 'Too' is the definition and 'much' joins the wave motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Too and as well both mean also or in addition, adverbs that can swap in a sentence.

clue.text: Avoids commitment when Shed, say, is playing tricks

indicators.note: playing tricks means messing about, so the letters are juggled

parts.note: taken as written
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means

explanation.surface: A garden shed that seems to be playing tricks, leaving someone unable to commit.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Shed' disguises a plain word; 'say' is the standard crossword way to give EG.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hedges gives evasive answers to avoid being pinned down to a position.

clue.text: Vegetable gum (ethically sourced)

indicators.note: something sourced is drawn out of something else, so letters are taken from inside the words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A gum made from plants and produced with fair, ethical standards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vegetable' looks like the definition, but in this puzzle the vegetables are never defined; it supplies letters instead: vegetab-LE GUM E-thically.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble hides the category, and a legume is a pod-bearing plant such as a pea or bean.

clue.text: See 17
Dispute after damage

indicators.note: what comes after is placed second in the answer

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or damage
a row is a quarrel

explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in reverse order in the clue, so 'after' puts the quarrel second.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble groups eleven answers, and the marrow, a large British summer squash, is one.

clue.text: Somewhere in the north (not the north)

indicators.note: not means without, so this letter is struck out

parts.note: a Scandinavian country in northern Europe
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A vague location up north, oddly said not to be in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: SWEDEN without its N. In Britain a swede is the yellow root Americans call a rutabaga.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition by design; the preamble hides the category, and the swede is a large yellow-fleshed root crop.

clue.text: Tragic result about one lost from nine miners

indicators.note: a tragic outcome is a wreck, so the letters are thrown into disorder
moved about means put in a different order
what is lost from a word no longer appears in it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before trimming
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: News of a mining disaster in which one of nine miners died.
explanation.walkthrough: NINE loses I to give NNE, and those letters with RESULT are rearranged. The grid uses the single-L American spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Miners dig shafts and galleries underground, so they are people who bore tunnels.

clue.text: Shiny little vegetable

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
the leek is an onion-family vegetable

explanation.surface: A small, glossy vegetable on display.
explanation.walkthrough: Little gives S, the clothing-size abbreviation for small.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleek hair or fur is smooth and glossy, which is to say it has a polished sheen.

clue.text: Fool that is not perturbed by Spain's first slave treaties

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: something perturbed is unsettled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: first keeps just the initial letter of the word

parts.note: the opening letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: A calm fool unmoved by the history of Spain's slave trade agreements.
explanation.walkthrough: An obscure word best built from its parts: ASS, IE, the rearranged NOT, and Spain's initial.
explanation.definitionFit: An asiento was a Spanish crown contract licensing another nation or company to supply African slaves to its colonies.
